strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework with formal proofs based on computational geometry and oriented matroid theory
Novel use of functional programming with strong typing to derive algorithms ensuring correctness
Well-motivated problem addressing interpretable ML for high-stakes applications
Clear logical progression from sequential decision processes to final algorithm
weaknesses: Polynomial time claim is misleading: algorithm runs in O(N^D) which is only polynomial for fixed D; for realistic D values this becomes prohibitively expensive

Severely inadequate experimental evaluation: only 5 small datasets (D≤6, N≤748), no wall-clock time comparisons with other exact methods (branch-and-bound, MIP solvers), and no comparison with previously designed related algorithms mentioned in paper
Extremely limited practical applicability: modern ML requires D in hundreds/thousands; restriction to D≤6 makes algorithm relevant only for toy problems

Limited novelty of core algorithmic insight: enumeration of O(N^D) hyperplanes through D points is based entirely on well-established Cover's dichotomies (1965); contribution is primarily in implementation rather than innovation

Insufficient algorithm specification for practice: impact of the approximate upper bound parameter on runtime not studied, numerical stability of linear system solving not analyzed, sensitivity to underflow threshold not investigated
Strong assumption of general position rarely satisfied in real data; no discussion of failure modes or behavior on nearly-degenerate data

Missing critical experiments: no scaling analysis with varying D, no sensitivity analysis on upper bound quality, no experiments on higher-dimensional datasets, constant factors in O(N^D) not characterized
Presentation heavy on functional programming notation may alienate ML researchers; balance between theory and practical impact is poor for an ML conference
